findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add tests/unit/test_snapshot_cache.py to Scope and update its comment at lines 166-168 so it describes the new deferred `_evict` contract. Also re-check `_evict`, `reverify_entry` and `GcResult` with find_referencing_symbols plus a string grep.
evidence: Plan: "`_evict` returns `None` (deferred) when the rename fails and the entry is still present; it returns 0 only when the entry is already gone."
Plan Scope lists tests/unit/test_snapshot_janitor.py but not tests/unit/test_snapshot_cache.py

tests/unit/test_snapshot_cache.py:166-168: "Windows refuses to rename a directory holding an open file. The janitor's _evict treats that OSError as \"nothing reclaimed\" and keeps the entry, so the live reader is protected by the refusal instead of by delete-on-close."
findings.finding: The plan changes what `_evict` does when the rename fails: today it returns 0 ('nothing reclaimed'); after the change it returns None ('deferred') and keeps the entry. tests/unit/test_snapshot_cache.py describes the old contract in a comment, and that file is not in the Scope list. After the change the comment misstates the Windows eviction path it documents.
scenarios: tests/unit/test_snapshot_cache.py::test_open_reader_survives_eviction_then_relookup_misses: after the change, its comment still says `_evict` treats the Windows rename failure as 'nothing reclaimed'. In fact the pass now reports the entry as deferred (`GcResult.deferred`), keeps its bytes and sidecars, and evicts it on a later pass. A future reader of this AC3 test would be misled about the contract the new janitor tests pin.
findings.suggested_fix: Add tests/unit/test_snapshot_cache.py to Scope and reword the comment at :166-168 to something like: "The janitor's _evict reports this as a deferred eviction (GcResult.deferred) and keeps the entry and its bytes; a later pass evicts it once the reader closes."

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] In (a), say how a corrupt entry that `reverify_entry` deferred is treated by `cache.acquire`'s hit path during the deferral: either record in ADR 0005 D3 / repo-snapshot-gates.md that it is still served until a later pass can move it (and that overlapping readers can keep deferring it), or have the hit path treat it as a miss.
evidence: Plan: "reverify_entry raises SnapshotEntryInUseError ... for a corrupt entry it could not move ... the next pass re-checks and evicts it"
src/rebar/_snapshot/cache.py:230-232 — `if dest.is_dir(): touch_entry(dest); return materialize(sha, ...)` reuses any entry present at the canonical path, with no check of integrity or deferral state
src/rebar/_snapshot/gc_trigger.py / janitor.start_background_janitor — the retry runs only once per interval_seconds (default 300)
findings.finding: The (a) design doesn't deal with the fact that a deferred entry stays at its canonical path, so `cache.acquire`'s hit path keeps serving it (and refreshes its mtime). For a corrupt entry that `reverify_entry` could not move, every gate on Windows keeps getting the corrupt content until a later pass finds no open handle. If gate runs overlap and keep the entry open, it may never get evicted. The plan says only that 'the next pass ... evicts it once the reader has closed it' and that the docs 'state the Windows deferral'. It doesn't say whether serving corrupt content during the deferral is accepted (and for how long), or whether a cache hit should treat a deferred corrupt entry as a miss.
findings.location: Second change (a) — reverify_entry / ADR 0005 D3 / docs/repo-snapshot-gates.md
scenarios: On a Windows host, a corrupt entry is held open by a running gate; reverify defers it; the gates that run before the next successful pass all read the corrupt snapshot.
On a busy Windows host, a corrupt entry is read by gate runs that overlap, so every pass finds a handle open and defers again, with no limit on how long this goes on.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State how readers are prevented from acquiring a corrupt entry whose eviction is deferred (e.g. readers check the unstamped/quarantine marker before use), and add a test that a new acquire after a deferral does not return the corrupt entry.
evidence: "`reverify_entry` raises `SnapshotEntryInUseError` ... for a corrupt entry it could not move"
"It leaves the integrity sidecar unstamped, so the next pass re-checks and evicts it."
findings.finding: While a corrupt entry is deferred on Windows, it stays at its canonical path. The plan does not say whether new readers are blocked from opening it during that window. Leaving the integrity sidecar unstamped only drives the next janitor pass. Separately, a steady stream of overlapping readers could keep the entry open indefinitely, so it is never moved. On POSIX, rename-to-trash removes the entry from the lookup path immediately.
scenarios: Windows: reader A holds a corrupt entry open; reverify defers it; reader B acquires the same entry from the canonical path and is served corrupt bytes.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State whether _reclaim_loop excludes a deferred entry from re-selection in the same pass and continues to younger candidates, and reconcile that with the 'next pass evicts it' claim.
evidence: "A deferred entry keeps its bytes in the running total and keeps its sidecars."
"_reclaim_loop counts a deferred entry there and does not count it as evicted or as freed space; the next pass ... evicts it once the reader has closed it."
findings.finding: The plan does not say how _reclaim_loop proceeds after a deferred entry. The deferred entry 'keeps its bytes in the running total', so the loop stays over budget. If the loop re-selects the oldest entry each iteration, it would pick the same deferred entry forever. If it skips to the next candidate, it over-evicts younger, unopened entries. In that case a later pass may already be under budget and never evict the deferred entry, which contradicts 'the next pass ... evicts it once the reader has closed it'.
scenarios: A reader holds the oldest entry open on Windows while the cache is over budget: the loop either spins on it or evicts several newer entries, after which the next pass finds the cache under budget and the deferred entry lingers.
findings.suggested_fix: Add: '_reclaim_loop marks a deferred entry as visited for this pass and continues to the next LRU candidate. Over-eviction of younger entries is accepted. A later pass evicts the formerly deferred entry only if it is still selected by LRU order or budget.' Alternatively, specify that the loop stops at the first deferred entry.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify that the red control reverts only the behavioural change (_evict/_reclaim_loop/reverify_entry semantics) while keeping SnapshotEntryInUseError and GcResult.deferred, and that the recorded failure is an assertion failure in test_eviction_rename_to_trash_open_reader_survives, not a collection or attribute error.
evidence: "a red control dispatch with the janitor.py change reverted (tests kept) shows test_eviction_rename_to_trash_open_reader_survives failing on Windows"
The tests are specified to use SnapshotEntryInUseError and the deferred field: "reverify_entry on a corrupt in-use entry raises SnapshotEntryInUseError", "the pass reports deferred == 1".
findings.finding: The red control dispatch reverts janitor.py but keeps the tests. The kept tests reference SnapshotEntryInUseError and GcResult.deferred, which the revert removes. A module-level import of SnapshotEntryInUseError would make tests/unit/test_snapshot_janitor.py fail at collection. test_eviction_rename_to_trash_open_reader_survives would then show as an error from ImportError or AttributeError, not as an assertion failure demonstrating the Windows rename behaviour. The control would appear red without proving what it claims.
findings.location: Testing — Second change, red control dispatch
scenarios: The revert removes the exception class, the module fails to import, and the JUnit XML shows a collection error for every janitor test.
findings.suggested_fix: Rewrite the red control as: revert only the _evict return-value and reverify_entry changes, keeping the new exception class and dataclass field. Confirm from the JUnit XML that test_eviction_rename_to_trash_open_reader_survives fails with an AssertionError.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State how the hidden-resource test makes peak_rss re-evaluate the import, for example monkeypatch sys.modules then importlib.reload(rebar.llm.peak_rss) with a restore in teardown, or confirm resource is imported lazily inside peak_rss_bytes().
evidence: "a new test hides resource (sys.modules["resource"] = None) on every platform and asserts the marker carries None for both"
findings.finding: The new peak-RSS test hides resource via sys.modules["resource"] = None. The plan does not say how peak_rss.py is made to observe this. If peak_rss imports resource once at module load (try/except at top level), setting sys.modules afterwards has no effect without importlib.reload or patching a module attribute. On POSIX the test would then see an int and fail. It might also pass only by accident on Windows.
findings.location: Second change (b) — new test hiding resource
scenarios: A Linux CI run of the new test: peak_rss already bound resource at import, so peak_rss_bytes() returns an int and the assertion fails.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] List every caller of _evict and reverify_entry (or state that _reclaim_loop and _reverify_pass are the only ones), and state how each handles None and SnapshotEntryInUseError, including precedence over any enclosing `except OSError`.
evidence: "_evict returns None (deferred) when the rename fails"
"reverify_entry raises SnapshotEntryInUseError (an OSError subclass ...) ... _reverify_pass catches it"
Only startup_sweep is explicitly cleared: "startup_sweep does not call _evict"
findings.finding: _evict's return type changes from int to Optional[int], and reverify_entry gains a new raised exception, an OSError subclass. The plan names only _reclaim_loop and _reverify_pass as the consumers that handle these. Any other caller would break or change behaviour silently: arithmetic on _evict's result (e.g. freed += _evict(...)) raises TypeError on None. A caller of reverify_entry outside _reverify_pass, or an outer broad `except OSError`, would swallow or mis-handle the new exception. No caller inventory is given.
findings.location: Second change (a) — _evict and reverify_entry contract changes
scenarios: A detached-trigger or CLI path calls reverify_entry directly and now crashes on a Windows in-use entry.
A helper sums _evict results and raises TypeError on None.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Enumerate every caller of `_evict` and `reverify_entry` and every consumer of `GcResult` (CLI/JSON/log output), and state how each handles `None`, `SnapshotEntryInUseError` and the new `deferred` field.
evidence: "`_evict` returns `None` (deferred) when the rename fails and the entry is still present"
"`reverify_entry` raises `SnapshotEntryInUseError` ... instead of returning True"
"`_reverify_pass` catches it ... so the pass never aborts" — no other callers enumerated
findings.finding: The plan changes `_evict`'s return contract (int → `None` when deferred) and `reverify_entry`'s contract (returns True → raises `SnapshotEntryInUseError`). It only names `_reclaim_loop` and `_reverify_pass` as consumers, and asserts only that `startup_sweep` does not call `_evict`. Any other caller would break: arithmetic on `None` raises TypeError, an uncaught OSError escapes, and a `GcResult` serializer or printer would not carry `deferred`.
scenarios: A heal-on-read or CLI path calls `reverify_entry` directly and now gets an uncaught OSError on Windows instead of True.
Code that sums `_evict` results gets `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'NoneType'`.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Log (or otherwise surface) each deferral with the entry and OSError, state whether `GcResult.deferred` is reported in the GC output, and define what happens when the same entry is deferred across many passes.
evidence: "A deferred entry keeps its bytes in the running total and keeps its sidecars."
"the next pass ... evicts it once the reader has closed it"
No log/metric/alert for deferrals is named
findings.finding: Deferral is unbounded and unobservable. Every rename failure with the entry still present is deferred and retried on the next pass forever, with no cap, log or warning. The plan names only a `GcResult.deferred` counter and does not say whether it is emitted anywhere. The entry's bytes stay in the running total, so a long-held reader keeps the cache over budget silently, and so does a permanent rename failure on any platform (e.g. EACCES on the trash dir).
scenarios: A long-lived process on Windows holds a snapshot file open: every GC pass reports deferred, nothing is logged, and the cache grows past its budget.
On POSIX, a misconfigured trash directory makes every rename fail permanently: entries that previously read as 'racing evictor' are now deferred forever with no signal.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a failure-disposition statement for the rename-failure arm: which OSError types are transient/deferred (retried next pass) and which are permanent and surfaced, for both `_evict` and `reverify_entry`.
evidence: "`_evict` returns `None` (deferred) when the rename fails and the entry is still present"
Tests only force `PermissionError`; no statement about other OSError subtypes
findings.finding: The plan alters a failure arm (a rename OSError in `_evict`/`reverify_entry`) but does not state its disposition contract. It never says which rename errors are treated as transient (Windows sharing violation / PermissionError from an open handle → deferred, retried next pass) versus permanent (other errno → surfaced/raised). As written, every rename failure with the entry still present maps to the transient 'deferred' disposition.
scenarios: A non-in-use failure (ENOSPC, EXDEV, EACCES on trash) is silently retried as 'deferred' rather than surfaced as a fatal error.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify that the new test reloads `rebar.llm.peak_rss` (or patches its bound `resource` attribute) under `monkeypatch.setitem(sys.modules, "resource", None)` and restores it afterwards.
evidence: "a new test hides `resource` (`sys.modules[\"resource\"] = None`) on every platform and asserts the marker carries `None` for both"
findings.finding: The new peak-RSS test hides `resource` with `sys.modules["resource"] = None`. That only takes effect if `peak_rss.py` imports `resource` at call time or the module is reloaded under the patch. The plan does not specify either. If `peak_rss.py` imports `resource` at module top, the test will not exercise the no-`resource` path on POSIX.
scenarios: On Linux, the test hides `resource` after `rebar.llm.peak_rss` has already bound it; `peak_rss_bytes()` still returns an int and the test fails, or gets rewritten into a weaker check.
findings.suggested_fix: Use `monkeypatch.setitem(sys.modules, "resource", None)` followed by `importlib.reload(peak_rss)`, plus a finalizer that reloads it again after the patch is undone; or `monkeypatch.setattr(peak_rss, "resource", None)` if the module binds it at import.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add tests/unit/test_snapshot_cache.py to Scope and update its Windows-branch comment (:166-168) to say `_evict` now reports the in-use entry as deferred (`GcResult.deferred`) and a later pass evicts it.
evidence: tests/unit/test_snapshot_cache.py:166-168: "Windows refuses to rename a directory holding an open file. The janitor's _evict treats that OSError as \"nothing reclaimed\" and keeps the entry, so the live reader is protected by the refusal instead of by delete-on-close."
Plan (a): "`_evict` returns `None` (deferred) when the rename fails and the entry is still present; it returns 0 only when the entry is already gone."
Plan Scope lists only tests/unit/test_snapshot_janitor.py among snapshot tests; test_snapshot_cache.py is absent.
findings.finding: The plan changes what `_evict` does on Windows: today it returns 0 ('nothing reclaimed'); under the plan it returns `None` and the pass counts the entry in `GcResult.deferred`. But `tests/unit/test_snapshot_cache.py` has a Windows-branch comment describing the current behaviour, and that file is not in the plan's Scope list. After the change the comment will describe behaviour that no longer exists.
scenarios: A maintainer reading the Windows branch of the cache test believes `_evict` silently reports nothing reclaimed, when the janitor now reports the entry as deferred and retries it on the next pass.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `tests/unit/test_snapshot_cache.py` (comment-only) to the Scope list, and reword lines 166-168 to: "Windows refuses to rename a directory holding an open file. The janitor's _evict reports that as deferred (GcResult.deferred) and keeps the entry and its bytes, so a later pass evicts it once the reader has closed it."
